claims.claim: Clive Staples Lewis was born in Belfast on November 29, 1898
Parents were Albert James Lewis and Florence Augusta (Flora) Lewis, born Hamilton; brother Warren, known as Warnie
He went by the name Jack from early childhood
His mother died of cancer on August 23, 1908, and he enrolled at Wynyard School in September 1908
Attended Campbell College, Cherbourg House, Malvern College, then tutored by William T. Kirkpatrick
Became an atheist at 15
Began at University College, Oxford, in 1917; commissioned in the 3rd Battalion, Somerset Light Infantry, on September 25, 1917
Wounded on April 15, 1918, during the Battle of Arras
Paddy Moore was killed in 1918; Lewis lived with and cared for Janie Moore until she was hospitalized in the late 1940s
Firsts in Honour Moderations (1920), Greats (1922) and English (1923)
Elected a Fellow of Magdalen College, Oxford, on May 20, 1925; held the fellowship until 1954
Accepted the Cambridge chair of Medieval and Renaissance Literature in 1954
Became a theist in 1929 and a Christian in 1931 after a discussion with Tolkien and Dyson
Member of the Inklings with J. R. R. Tolkien and Owen Barfield
The Pilgrim's Regress (1933), The Allegory of Love (1936), The Problem of Pain (1940), Surprised by Joy (1955)
Mere Christianity was compiled from BBC radio talks of 1941 to 1943
Seven Narnia books written 1949 to 1954; The Last Battle won the Carnegie Medal in 1956; over 100 million copies in 41 languages
Met Joy Davidman Gresham in September 1952
Civil marriage on April 23, 1956, at the register office, 42 St Giles', Oxford, after her visitor's visa was not renewed by the Home Office
Cancer found in October 1956 with bone metastases; bedside ceremony on March 21, 1957, by the Reverend Peter Bide; cancer returned October 1959; Greece holiday April 1960
Joy Davidman died on July 13, 1960, in Oxford, aged 45
A Grief Observed was published in 1961 by Faber and Faber under the pseudonym N. W. Clerk, drawn from four notebooks, with his wife called H., and republished under Lewis's name in 1963
Lewis died of kidney failure on November 22, 1963, aged 64, at The Kilns, one week before his 65th birthday, the day of the Kennedy assassination
Buried at Holy Trinity Church, Headington Quarry
Memorial stone dedicated in Poets' Corner, Westminster Abbey, on November 22, 2013

quotes.text: No one ever told me that grief felt so like fear.
My idea of God is not a divine idea. It has to be shattered time after time. He shatters it Himself. He is the great iconoclast.
I was getting from it the only pleasure a man in anguish can get; the pleasure of hitting back.

uncertain: Date and place of the religious marriage ceremony: Wikipedia (Lewis and Davidman articles) gives March 21, 1957, at her hospital bed (Churchill Hospital), and the C.S. Lewis Institute gives 1957; the C.S. Lewis Foundation chronology, as read through the fetch tool, placed a church marriage in December 1956 at Wingfield Hospital. The profile uses March 21, 1957, and names no hospital.

All three quotes were read through a summarizing fetch tool on the C.S. Lewis Institute page, a secondary article quoting the book. Run a mechanical exact-string check against that page before publishing; the primary text itself was not fetched.

Publication years for The Screwtape Letters, the printed Mere Christianity volume, and The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe were not cleanly confirmed in fetched pages, so the prose omits them. The year 1952 for Mere Christianity in primarySources is not confirmed by a fetched page and should be checked or removed.
Nationality is given as British; sources describe him as born in Belfast, Ireland, and he is sometimes described as Irish or Anglo-Irish.
Britannica, Poetry Foundation, the Wade Center and the HarperCollins official Lewis page could not be fetched (403 or blocked), so they are not cited.
The legacy sentence that many popular lines attributed to Lewis cannot be traced to his writing comes from the task brief, not from a fetched page; remove it if a source is required.
The statement that A Grief Observed differs in tone from The Problem of Pain is a characterization, supported only loosely by the C.S. Lewis Institute article.
